{{Short description|British academic (1931–2024)}}
{{for|the Jewish author and leader|Bernard G. Richards}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2018}}
{{Use British English|date=April 2018}}
'''Bernard Richards''' (16 October 1931 – 7 April 2024) was a British [[computer scientist]] and an Emeritus Professor of [[Medical Informatics]] at the [[University of Manchester]], England.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.manchester.ac.uk/research/bernard.richards/ | title=Prof Bernard Richards – personal details | publisher=[[The University of Manchester]] | accessdate=23 January 2018 }}</ref><ref name=":0" />

Richards studied mathematics and physics for his bachelor's degree.<ref name="copeland17">{{cite book| authorlink=Jack Copeland | last1=Copeland | first1=Jack | authorlink2=Jonathan Bowen | last2=Bowen | first2=Jonathan | last3=Sprevak | first3=Mark | authorlink4=Robin Wilson (mathematician) | last4=Wilson | first4=Robin |display-authors=et al | title=[[The Turing Guide]] | publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] | year=2017 | isbn=978-0198747833 | pages=478 | chapter=Notes on Contributors }}</ref> For his master's degree, he worked under the supervision of  [[Alan Turing]] (1912–1954) at Manchester as one of Turing's last students, helping to validate Turing’s theory of [[morphogenesis]].<ref>{{citation| last=Richards | first=Bernard | year=1954 | title=The Morphogenesis of Radiolaria | work=MSc thesis | publisher=[[The University of Manchester]] | location=Manchester, UK }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal| last=Richards | first=Bernard | year=2005 | title=Turing, Richards and morphogenesis | journal=[[The Rutherford Journal]] | volume=1 | url=http://www.rutherfordjournal.org/article010109.html }}</ref><ref>{{cite book| last=Richards | first=Bernard | year=2017 | chapter=Chapter 35 – Radiolaria: Validating the Turing theory | editor-last1=Copeland | editor-first1=Jack |editor-link1=Jack Copeland  |display-editors=etal| title=[[The Turing Guide]] | pages=383–388 }}</ref> Morphogenesis had been actively discussed in Manchester, in an empirical way, since 1919, before the availability of electronic computing.<ref> Manchester Memoirs VOLUME  LXIV (1919-20) Memoirs and Proceedings OF THE Manchester Literary & Philosophical Society </ref>

Reflecting on Turing's death at the age of 80 during Turing's centenary year in 2012, Richards commented: "The day he died felt like driving through a tunnel and the lights being switched off".<ref name=":0">{{cite news| url=https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/news/greater-manchester-news/alan-turing-the-day-he-died-689846 | title=Alan Turing: 'The day he died felt like driving through a tunnel and the lights being switched off' | newspaper=[[Manchester Evening News]] | date=19 June 2012 | accessdate=23 January 2018 | first=David | last=Henry }}</ref>

After Turing died, Richards changed his research area and worked for his doctorate, studying an aspect of [[optics]], resulting in a [[Royal Society]] paper with his supervisor, Professor [[Emil Wolf]].<ref name="copeland17" /> This provided a detailed description of the diffraction of light through a [[convex lens]]. After this, Richards moved into the area of medicine, producing an important paper on hormone peaks in the [[menstrual cycle]]. Later he worked on [[expert system]]s aimed at use in [[open heart surgery]] and also [[intensive care unit]]s.

Richards became Professor of [[Medical Informatics]] at Manchester University and latterly Emeritus Professor in the School of Computer Science.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.cs.manchester.ac.uk/about-us/staff/profile/?ea=bernard.richards | title=Prof Bernard Richards – personal details | publisher=School of Computer Science, [[The University of Manchester]] | accessdate=23 January 2018 }}</ref>

Richards served as a Chairman of the [[British Computer Society|BCS]] Health Informatics Committee and in 1998 was made BCS Fellow of the Year for Services to Medical Informatics.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.bcs.org/upload/pdf/brichards_efmi_statement.pdf | title=My Statement re EFMI Rep | publisher=[[British Computer Society|BCS]] |first=Bernard | last=Richards | accessdate=23 January 2018 }}</ref> He was the first President of the [[Institute for Health Record and Information Management]] (IHRIM), a member of the [[International Federation of Records Officers]] (IFRO). In [[Europe]], he is an Honorary Member of the [[Ukrainian Association for Computer Medicine]] of [[Ukraine]], the [[Romania]]n Academy of Medical Science, the [[John von Neumann Computer Society]] of [[Hungary]], the [[Czech Republic|Czech]] Medical Informatics Society, and the [[Poland|Polish]] Medical Informatics Society. Richards was presented with an award by [[Queen Elizabeth II]] for contributing a morphogenesis memento to a [[time capsule]] during 2012, Alan Turing's centenary year.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/the-northerner/2013/jan/22/alan-turing-computing | title=Alan Turing Year – the Establishment still doesn't get it | newspaper=[[The Guardian]] | authorlink=S. Barry Cooper | first=S. Barry | last=Cooper | date=22 January 2013 }}</ref>

Richards died on 7 April 2024, at the age of 92.<ref>{{cite web |title=In Memoriam – Bernard Richards (1931 – 2024) |url=https://www.bibliomed.org/mnsfulltext/220/220-1719146998.pdf?1726665840 |website=bibliomed.org |access-date=18 September 2024}}</ref>
